# ShiftLead — design history

The dated record of how [`design.md`](design.md) came to say what it says: decisions, reversals,
review rounds, live findings and Paul's words, by section, in date order. `design.md` is the
present-tense specification and states only what is true now; this file is where its history went
on 2026-09-22 (the design review, TD-109) and where every later change appends its dated fact.
Nothing here is a rule. Where a bullet and the design disagree, the design is current and the
bullet is what was true on its date.

The ADRs under [`decisions/`](decisions/) and the ledger ([`technical_debt.md`](technical_debt.md),
[`technical_debt_archive.md`](technical_debt_archive.md)) hold the reasoning behind the larger
decisions; this file points at them rather than repeating them.

## Title and status

- 2026-10-10 (TD-060 step 2, the anchor; Paul, that day: `agentorc` → `shiftlead` for the distribution, the product package, its console scripts and entry-point group, the state directory, the `SHIFTLEAD_*` variables, the units and the venv; `sessionorc` kept; a clean cut with `ao migrate`; a repo's `.agentorc.yml` read as a fallback until it renames its own): the machine names carry the project's name. The command stays `ao` and the session prefix `ao-`; the repo is to be renamed `shiftlead` as well (Paul, the same evening), a later step.
- 2026-10-06 (TD-351, grinder-ao-2, PR #1172): the split landed — `scripts/split_design.py` moved the design into thirty files under `docs/design/`, nothing reflowed and a relative link's path given `../`; `docs/design.md` became the index; the doc-bound tests read through `tests/design_doc.py`; the briefs point their greps at `docs/design/`.
- 2026-10-06 (TD-346, the designer; Paul, that day: *do it, in a quiet window*): the layout of the split decided — thirty files under `docs/design/` named `<§>-<slug>.md`, one per section and per §4 subsection, each beginning with its heading line as it stands; `design.md` the index; this history kept one file; tests through `tests/design_doc.py`; the move a script, landed when no open PR touches the file. Not built — TD-351.
- 2026-09-04: the design session that produced this document; the project was called `sessionherd` for most of that day (see §10 for the rename to agentorc).
- 2026-09-05: the last of the original open questions closed; building started the same day.
- 2026-09-21: Paul named the project ShiftLead (shiftlead.dev). The packages, state directory, units, config file and command home keep the `agentorc` name until TD-060's second step, at a release boundary.
- Until 2026-09-22 the Status paragraph read "phase 1 in progress", listing the host agent, the Claude Code adapter, the Org and Focus pages, New session and the CLI as running.

## 1. Problem

- 2026-08-07: the samscrape stranded-work audit that, with `tdgrind` (TD-274), supplied the lessons listed in §1 (reboot killed tmux, OAuth lapses, pane-grepped state, reports lost in scrollback, chat-only work lost on close).

## 2. Goals

- 2026-10-09 (TD-464, the designer; the second pass, slice 14): goal 12's two TD-038 markers left for this record (the Dark Modern palette and the WebGL renderer are TD-038's).
- 2026-09-13 (TD-038): the Focus pane took VS Code's Dark Modern terminal palette as literals, not tokens, so the pane does not follow the page.
- 2026-09-20 (TD-038): the Focus pane's face became bundled JetBrains Mono (OFL, ligatures off) and it draws through xterm.js's WebGL renderer where available, DOM renderer otherwise.

## 3. Prior art

- 2026-09-04: the original survey (ttyd, ccmanager, claude-squad, Vibe Kanban, agent-dashboard, Anthropic Remote Control). At that point multi-host was itself a differentiator.
- 2026-09-05: ttyd's websocket-around-a-pty shape was superseded by a bridge inside the UI process, since the pty would wrap `ssh` anyway (§10).
- 2026-09-09: herdr added to the survey (not in the 2026-09-04 survey). Herdr, Inc. announced a $6M seed (Bessemer, YC) the same day; "Herdr Cloud" (no-ssh machines) was next; releases 0.5.1 (2026-04) → 0.9.0 (2026-09); 36.5k stars, ~770k installs; ~1k community plugins found by a GitHub topic, no review; 17 integrations of which six (Pi, OMP, Kimi, OpenCode, Kilo, MastraCode) push state from hooks; single binary for macOS, Linux, Windows; Claude rate-limit and context bars; features via Discussions, bugs fixed by the maintainers' own agent, an allow-list of approved contributors.
- 2026-09-10: herdr entry corrected and herdr measured as a substrate ([ADR](decisions/2026-09-10-herdr-spike.md)); not taken. Since herdr, multi-host on its own stopped being a differentiator. Its restore model is layout + `claude --resume`; its `pane.agent_status_changed` event carries only the state (the `--message` of a report is stored nowhere); community mobile apps exist, the TUI over ssh is its mobile story.
- 2026-09-10: OpenAI's Agents API entered public beta. Its stateful predecessor, the Assistants API, had sunset 2026-08-26. Environments could be OpenAI-hosted or Cloudflare / Vercel / Oracle / E2B / Modal / Daytona / DigitalOcean / Blaxel / Runloop; progress by streaming or webhooks; managed context compaction and subagent delegation; token billing, no infrastructure fee.
- 2026-09-12: the orchestrator-membership prior-art survey (supervision trees, owner references, unit relationships, capability attenuation, ACL placement) for the §10 question ([ADR](decisions/2026-09-12-orchestrator-membership-prior-art.md)).
- 2026-09-13: OpenAI's Agents API surveyed and added ([ADR](decisions/2026-09-13-openai-agents-api.md)).
- 2026-09-16: agent messaging surveyed (Claude Code cross-session messaging and agent teams, mcp_agent_mail, muster / agent-mux / muxcode) ([ADR](decisions/2026-09-16-agent-messaging-prior-art.md)).
- 2026-09-20 (TD-059): session desks and supervisors surveyed (agentboss, agent-director, multi-agent-shogun, claude-code-orchestrator, tmux_claude_codex_dashboard, orchardist) ([ADR](decisions/2026-09-20-session-desk-neighbours.md)).
- 2026-10-13 (Paul): Grok Bot surveyed ([ADR](decisions/2026-10-13-grok-bot.md)): it takes the "org of agents" concept for office work on a vendor cloud, with the model routed by the vendor (Claude Opus 5.5 among them, announced 2026-10-07, no picker, not bring-your-own-key); not the job of driving the person's own coding agents in their repos.
- 2026-10-13 (Paul): Muse surveyed ([ADR](decisions/2026-10-13-muse.md)): Meta's consumer agent on Meta's cloud and models, which shares only the works-while-away, asks-for-approval loop; its sibling Muse Code is a harness shiftlead could run, not a rival. The Grok Bot ADR gained *Can it run with shiftlead?*: no inbound API, and a Bot driving `ao` or the UI would act as the person.
- 2026-10-13 (Paul): Hermes Agent surveyed ([ADR](decisions/2026-10-13-hermes-agent.md)): the nearest of the day's three — open source, self-hosted and model-neutral, with a Kanban board of workers that review, use worktrees and complete on a PR's required checks; it differs in being its own harness (headless workers, one host, Claude Max only through extra usage), so shiftlead could run it as a tool rather than be replaced by it.
- 2026-10-13 (Paul): the three surveys' lessons gathered for discussion ([ADR](decisions/2026-10-13-agent-product-lessons.md)), judged by Paul's two differentiators — taking control of a live terminal session, and running on the person's own subscriptions — and his read that a person uses either Hermes or shiftlead, not both. Paul's answers the same day: a director seat to answer permission prompts (TD-636), no *done* on a red PR (TD-637), the model in a commit's attribution (TD-638), the Inbox as the phone's text interface before any chat app, Gemini CLI as the next tool; the other five declined.

## 4.1 Session substrate: tmux, one session per conversation
- 2026-10-24 (TD-995, the designer): `ao msg`'s *no session named* refusal names `--team` / `--repo`. Built by TD-1000.
- 2026-10-24 (TD-979 slice 2, the techlead's review of #2312): *Kept, and said* lists the two whys the build writes that it did not: *git state unknown* and *the reap failed: <error>*. A pane still there at the deadline reads *timed out*. A string `reap` that came over the link is the home's whoever closed, so a session's routed close of a container node's member is never refused for it.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 19, Fable, NOT READY, 1 medium and 3 nits, every one a follow-on of round 18, all adopted; the loop ends, Sonnet having said READY in round 16 and 18's findings being its own retry's): git still registers a directory removed by hand, so the retry reads the checked-out branch from `worktree list --porcelain`, prunes, then weighs it and the launch branch, as the stamp's recovery does. The local branch is read as `refs/heads/<b>`.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 18, Sonnet, NOT READY, 2 medium, 3 low and a nit, all adopted, no loss path found): `branch_kept` is a map of branch to why, so the retry reads names, not prose, and rewrites it. The retry runs on the record's host under the per-name worktree lock, bounded, so it never deletes a branch a create is checking out. It also covers a directory the person removed by hand. The default branch is skipped silently. §4.7's retry sentence gets its own paragraph.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 17, Fable, NOT READY, 1 medium, 2 low and a nit, all adopted): a reaped record has no directory, so `ao close`'s retry never reached a kept branch; it now weighs `branch_kept`'s branches again, the road back after `set-head` or a rebase after the close. A branch that no longer exists is skipped. The migration's marking of a hand-started unattended team session is named as an accepted edge, since no commit is lost.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 16, Sonnet, READY, 3 low and 2 nits, all adopted, every branch case run in scratch repos): a rebase after the close is named beside one before it; reachable reflog values expire at 90 days and a repo with `core.logAllRefUpdates` off keeps none, both on the safe side; *no origin/HEAD* names `git remote set-head origin -a` as its cure.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 15, Fable, NOT READY, 1 medium, 3 low and 2 nits, five of them follow-ons of round 14, all adopted): `for-each-ref` given the short name `origin/HEAD` lists nothing, so round 14's list would have left `origin/HEAD` out. The test is now `git rev-list <b> --not --remotes=origin` plus the reflog's values when `git reflog exists`: every `origin` ref that exists, with nothing to list by hand, so a launch branch whose commits went out on a topic branch cut from it is freed too. `origin` and `origin/HEAD` are read first, in order.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 14, Sonnet, NOT READY, 1 high, 2 low and 2 nits, all adopted, run in scratch repos): `rev-list` fails on a missing `origin/<b>`, so a never-pushed branch was kept by error, not weighed. The `--not` list is now only the refs that exist (`for-each-ref`) and the reflog when there is one, and a failed read keeps as *could not be weighed*. `branch -D`'s refusal reads *checked out in <path>*. The default branch is set aside before the test. The whole reflog is read, not `--fork-point`'s cut, and the branch step is bounded as a whole.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 13, Fable, NOT READY, 1 high, 1 medium, 3 low and 2 nits, all adopted, git's behaviour checked in scratch repos): `origin/HEAD` joins the refs a branch's tip may be reached from, so a launch branch never pushed and with no commit of its own is deleted, and a refill never resumes it at a stale base. The test is one `rev-list` per branch, bounded as one step. *no origin* and *no origin/HEAD* are `branch_kept` whys. Expired reflog entries keep, *unlocked* is read before `--dehydrate`, and a deleted branch is named in `branches_deleted`.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978, Paul's review of the loop after round 12, Sonnet's READY on the patch-id text set aside): the worktree and the branch get separate tests, each git's own where git has one. Removing a worktree loses no commit, since its branch keeps them, so the worktree is weighed by files and occupants only: git's `worktree remove` refusal plus the reaper's *clean*, *idle* and *nested*. The branch is deleted once origin has held its tip: `git branch -d`'s ancestry test against `origin/<b>`, widened by that ref's reflog as `--fork-point` reads it, so a rebase before the close, clean or not, frees the branch. Rounds 8 to 12's patch-id twins, the reap's fetch and its lock, and the stamp's verdicts are gone. A kept branch is `branch_kept` and never keeps the worktree.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 11, Fable, NOT READY, 1 high, 1 medium, 1 low, every one a follow-on of round 10, and a nit, all adopted, checked in a scratch repo): a `-U0` patch-id drops where a hunk lands, so round 10's pool let a pushed commit vouch for an unpushed one adding the same lines elsewhere. The pool now leaves out every commit HEAD holds (`origin/<branch> --not <default> HEAD`, as `git cherry` reads it), `<default>` read as the reaper reads it, and a checkout without one keeps. The reaping stamp holds each branch's whole delete verdict, since `update-ref -d` checks no worktree, and the recovery prunes first.
- 2026-10-23 (TD-978's review, round 10, Sonnet, NOT READY, 1 high, 2 medium, 2 low and a nit, all adopted, the pushed test run in scratch repos): a twin is sought only among the branch's own commits on origin (`origin/<branch> --not origin/HEAD`), one origin commit per local one, so an older commit a revert of a revert repeats never vouches; an empty patch-id never matches. The patch-id is read from a `-U0` diff, so a clean rebase over an edit near the change keeps it. Only `origin`'s refs are read. `worktree_reaping` holds each branch's verdict and tip, and a recovery deletes by compare (`update-ref -d <b> <oid>`) and prunes. A rebase that dropped a commit keeps.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 9, Fable, NOT READY, 5 findings, every one a follow-on of round 8, all adopted): round 8's `git cherry` skipped merge commits and ignored whitespace, so a merge could have been deleted. *pushed* is now that every commit `rev-list` names has an exact twin on `origin/<branch>` by `git patch-id --verbatim`; a merge, an absent `origin/<branch>` or a detached HEAD keeps. Branch reads come before `--dehydrate`, and the one `branch -D` is exempt from the deadline, so a late remove still frees the branch. A stamp found with the directory gone becomes `worktree_reaped_at`.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 8, Sonnet, NOT READY, 12 findings with no high, all adopted): a commit patch-equivalent to one on `origin/<branch>` counts as pushed, so a clean rebase before the close is reaped too; that is #2292's own order, and TD-978's *Done when* says so. The lock section is shielded from cancellation, and each lock wait is bounded (*busy*). `worktree_made` is tri-state, migrated only when absent, and inherited by any create that supersedes. Only a Resume bases on `origin/<name>`. The re-hydrate is exempt from the deadline, and `worktree_reaping` catches a killed reap (*interrupted*). Outside sessions that are ShiftLead's are skipped. A string `reap` comes only from a call with no session caller. TD-979's tests and a note to dev-cadence are added.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 7, Fable, NOT READY, 7 findings, every one a follow-on of rounds 5 and 6, all adopted): the migration marks only `unattended` team records. A sharing host whose link is down keeps the worktree. `--dehydrate` never starts past 40 s, so the close answers by 100 s. Both locks key by the main checkout. A `fetch:<repo>` lock serialises ShiftLead's fetches. An unpushed why reads *n commits on no remote ref*. TD-979's record line agrees with the migration.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 6, Sonnet, NOT READY, 1 medium and 1 low, both adopted): `rpc_create` takes the directory's lock before letting the worktree's go, so no reap runs between a create's `ensure_worktree` and its pane. The reap runs `git fetch --prune origin` first, so a remote branch deleted unmerged no longer vouches for its commits. A failed fetch keeps the worktree.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 5, Fable, NOT READY, 8 findings, all adopted): the build marks once every record that holds a `worktree` and a `team` as made, or no seat live at the build would ever be reaped. *idle* takes `occupants`' host set with its own filter (any adapter, inside), and `external_sessions()` reports its blind adapters, which keep. A kept record's `worktree_kept` clears on a directory-existence check, not a git read. A surviving local launch branch is checked out as it stands. The departure from cadence §1.2 is named. The tick's own closes wait for their reap, accepted. A scheduled start inherits as well.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 4, Sonnet, NOT READY, 9 findings, all adopted): `DISPOSABLE_IGNORED` (tool caches, `*.egg-info`, a real `.venv`) joins the reaper's exemptions. This departs from the synced reaper knowingly, since every worker that ran its tests holds those caches. The reap takes the directory's lock after the worktree's, so a create reusing the worktree is never cut. It never counts the closing record itself, and it runs after the `closed` save. Each step is bounded by `REAP_STEP` (20 s) under the 120 s link. `ensure_worktree` fetches with `--prune` and never revives a stale `origin/<name>`. `reap: bool | str`. Older records have no `worktree_made` and are removed by hand.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 3, Fable, NOT READY, 10 findings, 9 of them follow-ons of round 2, all adopted): a restart's or Resume's record inherits `worktree_made` from the record it supersedes, so a restarted member's close still reaps; any other found worktree reads *not made here*. `REAP_WITHIN` is a deadline the thread reads between steps, and the close holds the lock until it returns and answers after it. `reap` is `True`, `False` (a restart) or a why string. *idle* is ported through `occupants`' records and `external_sessions()`, not dev-cadence's registry. A Cancel's kept worktree is said in its reply. `ao close` retries on any made, still-present worktree and keeps the close stamps. §4.8's rename sentence is reconciled.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978, the designer's steers to the techlead): m-f13b516ebe22 (detach and delete the branch only) was answered *go with your default* (m-f710a053894a). m-68633ab3e0e1 corrected it before that round's text landed, and was answered *go with your default: Close removes the worktree ShiftLead made behind reap_worktrees.sh's guards* (m-189e81814566), which replaces the first reply.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 2, Sonnet, NOT READY, 13 findings, all adopted; the designer's steers m-f13b516ebe22, then m-68633ab3e0e1 correcting it): narrowing the fix to detaching HEAD and deleting the branch was weighed and dropped, because `reap_worktrees.sh` never reaps a detached worktree. The close's tests become the reaper's *clean* (ignored files included, its exemptions named), *idle*, *unlocked* and *nested*, with a strict *pushed* (`rev-list --not --remotes`) for *landed*, one measure for the worktree and its branches. All run read-only before `--dehydrate`. Only a worktree the start created is reaped (`worktree_made`). The reap runs under the create's per-name lock, after the pane is gone, bounded by `REAP_WITHIN`. The home checks live records across nodes. A recreated launch branch bases on `origin/<name>`. The one-press Resume sends `repo` as `dir`. `worktree_kept` and `worktree_reaped_at` are defined. `ao close` on a kept record retries the reap. A missing `reap` over the link reaps. A scheduled Cancel reaps. TD-979's tests are listed in full, and Close's help text changes in the build.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978's review, round 1, Fable, NOT READY, 10 findings, all adopted): `git worktree remove` deletes ignored files and nested checkouts silently. So a dev-cadence checkout's `hydrate_worktree.sh --check` and `--dehydrate` run first, and without the script any nested `.git` keeps the worktree. Every close reaps but a restart's; the list is examples. An exited shell does not hold the worktree. A failed restart's closed record is the stranded-work sweep's. The one-press Resume carries `worktree`. A rebase before the close keeps the worktree and is the person's. A reaped record draws *reaped* and no git views.
- 2026-10-22 (TD-978, the designer; from #2195 and #2292, where a closed member's stale local branch failed the gate's `pushed` row after another session rebased its PR): *A close reaps the worktree*. The person's Close, rule 9's closes, a seat's close and `ao team stop --close` remove the worktree ShiftLead made, plus its checked-out branch and its launch branch. They do this only when the tree is clean, every commit is on a remote-tracking ref, and no live record works inside it. A restart's close keeps it. A kept worktree's `worktree_kept` says why. Detaching HEAD was not taken, since the gate reads the local branch ref. Build TD-979.

- 2026-10-21 (TD-952, grinder-ao-2; main's CI failed `test_a_supervised_create_on_a_node_leaves_its_launch_record_at_the_home` on 20e7283): a pane the host agent's own create is still starting is never adopted. `create` starts the tmux session in a thread and puts the record in after; a tick in that gap adopted the pane as a nameless `shell`, and on a node the adoption reached the home before the create's reply, so the home refused the real record as another session and wrote no launch record. Reproduced 7 in 300 under load; 300 of 300 with the fix.
- 2026-10-21 (#2249; Paul, from a session opened on a Queue card: *I don't think the "shiftlead.." portion of the prompt is needed, and it feels odd to see it as a user*): the brief's typed line is in the person's voice, *My brief for this session is pasted below; read it and act on it.*, where it was *shiftlead: the text pasted below is your brief from the person who started this session; read it and act on it*, and the preface describes it so; the line is the same for every starter, a lead or director starting a member too, since the person sent the text deliberately, by pressing the button or by a policy they set. Not taken: dropping the line for sessions opened from the Queue, which would rest TD-343's cure on the preface and the tool's handling of a bare paste alone.
- 2026-10-15 (TD-717, the designer; a techlead seat filled five seconds before an auto promote lost its first hook and sat eight hours at an empty composer): *A launch whose hook never comes is recovered*. The scraped send keys on the composer reading empty, not on a scraped `idle`, which Claude Code's empty composer never gives. The record keeps `hook_seen_at`, and only that seeds the agent's fresh-hook table at load, since every new Claude Code record is `confidence: hook` from its create and a restart counted its missing hook as fresh (the 47-minute mark). A supervised record marked *no hook since launch* is replayed once, with its askers told. No screen rule for the empty composer, and no coupling between a promote and a fill. Built by TD-720.
- 2026-10-10 (TD-060 step 2, the anchor): `install --system` stops and removes the old-named system units first, refused while their server holds a session.
- 2026-10-09 (TD-495 slice 2, grinder-ao-1): `ao service install` gains the tmux system unit's text (`service.tmux_unit_text`). It stages the text at `~/.agentorc/systemd/agentorc-tmux.service` and prints *run once as root: sudo <ao> service install --system* only when `/etc/systemd/system`'s copy is absent or differs. The `ao` path is absolute, since root's PATH has no venv. `--system` refuses a non-root caller, naming that line. As root it makes the text again for `SUDO_USER`. It never copies the stage: any session can write that file, and root would run what it says (review). It is refused while a server other than the unit's answers on the person's socket. Then it runs `daemon-reload` and `enable --now`. The unit carries `LANG=C.UTF-8`, and its tmux is the first one the agent unit's PATH finds. `ao service status` adds where the server runs, in §4.7's words.
- 2026-10-09 (TD-489, the designer): the root press installs the watch timer beside the tmux unit. Built by TD-497.
- 2026-10-09 (TD-488, the designer; the outage of 2026-10-09 12:30–16:50, TD-489's kill of `systemd --user`): **the installed home's tmux server is a system unit**, `agentorc-tmux.service` with `User=` the person, `tmux -D`, `Delegate=yes`, root-installed once by the person with `sudo ao service install --system` from the text `ao service install` writes under `~/.agentorc/systemd/`. Until this date the server was the daemon the host agent started from inside `agentorc-agent.service` (kept there by `KillMode=process`), so it outlived the agent's restart and died with the user manager: at 12:30:53 one SIGTERM to `systemd --user` (pid 1920) ran `exit.target`, which SIGKILLed the server and every session on kmaster, and nothing restarted them until an ssh login at 16:50:26. The host agent's and the UI's units stay user units — a promote restarts them unprivileged, and TD-489's alarm covers their absence; all three as system units was weighed and not taken. Steered to Paul as `m-67567527ee50`. Built by TD-495.
- 2026-10-09 (TD-464, the designer; the second pass, slice 13): §4.1 cut to the substrate's rules — what left: the suspension exception's TD-077 (a2); the *show command runs* box retired by TD-418; *No prose in the argv* designed 2026-10-05, built by TD-339 slices 2 and 1, and its incident — on 2026-10-05 a repo script a member was told to run ended with `pkill -f chromium`, matched the word in the brief riding in that member's own argv, and killed the session running it; *The brief is the person's word* designed 2026-10-06, built by TD-347 slices 1 and 2, after a seat on 2026-10-06 answered its brief that it held only pasted text and held a PR ask ten hours, its *Done when* on a scratch home on Opus and on Fable; *A brief whose first hook is lost* designed 2026-10-06, built by TD-348, after one sat at an empty composer 7.5 hours; 2,600 → 2,521 words.
- undated (PR #17): Resume's supersede — closes the exited record and keeps it a day. The create-time supersede (below) extends it to a fresh start under the same name and goes one step further by forgetting rather than keeping.
- undated: `pipe-pane` continuous streaming to `~/.agentorc/runs/<session>-<created>.log` replaced tdgrind's per-tick snapshot.
- 2026-09-10 (§10 decision, §9 invariant 12): a name identifies one session within its scope (the repo, or the directory for a repo-less session).

A paste refused after the line went in is known from the step that failed (`LeadTyped`), and the next try pastes the brief after the line: reading the line back does not work, since Claude Code paints the 111-character line over two rows of an 80-column pane and the composer read returns the first (the techlead's reading of PR #1158). Decided in the build: the file is named by the conversation id, not the tmux name the design first gave, because the adapter's launch runs before the host agent picks the tmux name (it may retry on tmux's own *duplicate session*); it is removed when the last record holding the conversation is forgotten, since a Resume of that conversation hands it again; and a resume id that is not a plain file name is refused rather than written outside `launch/`.

Decided in the build: the doorbell is held off while a brief is due, since its line would otherwise be the session's first prompt; a retry presses Enter again on a composer still holding the last try's brief rather than typing it twice (§4.2); a dialog or someone's words in the composer waits uncounted; and any `UserPromptSubmit` ends the brief's wait — a person's own first prompt included — since the hook carries the word `prompt`, never the text. The mark is the card's slot in the needs family's amber (its colour, never its ring) and a Focus header badge `#fbrief` beside *paused · usage*, kept current from the delta.

## 4.2a Profiles: tool · account · model

An `ask` carrying such a PR sends with the line *checks never started on <head>: <reason>*, since §4.9b names no refusal for it. `promote.read_checks` returns a third value, `checks_not_run`, kept on the promote reading with the checkout's `origin`, the jobs' verdicts cached per checkout and sha. `workorders.ci_not_run(repos, promotes)` groups both by owner in lower case, for TD-687. A PR red at the last reading that turns `not_run` and conflicting starts its `red_since` afresh, since its order is by the conflict alone (the techlead's note on #1766).
- 2026-10-14 (TD-686 slice 1, grinder-ao-1): *CI that never started is the person's* — the reading's half built. In a repo whose `origin` is GitHub, a red PR's failing Actions jobs are read in order (`reports.classify_failing`, at most `JOBS_CAP` fifty, stopping at the first that started or could not be read), and a PR whose failing items all never started reads `checks: not_run` with `not_run: {reason, kind, runs}`, the verdicts kept as `jobs: {head, read}`. It gets no `red_since` save from a conflict; a conflicting one's order says *conflicting · CI never ran*. A sync PR `not_run` and not conflicting waits (`is_sync_order`), its `sync_since` taken afresh each reading, so a conflict starts its order's clock; its reason adds *CI never ran*. The Repo page tags it *CI never ran*, its hover the reason, and the team card counts it apart (*· n CI never ran*). The `done`'s read, the promote's checks and `ci_not_run` are slice 2's.

- Until 2026-09-20 the usage poll ran every minute; TD-087 moved it to five minutes because a minute buys nothing against a five-hour window while spending an allowance the tool itself shares. The stated cost: a session at its cap shows `limited` up to five minutes later rather than up to one.
- 2026-09-20 (TD-087): usage fetch failures gained a reason. Before, *rate-limited*, *no credentials*, *no network* and *no profile* were one silence, and the silence cost more than a missing chip: `limited` is read from the same reading, so a session at its cap was not marked while the endpoint refused us. The `Retry-After` from a 429 is honoured uncapped because "a server saying *an hour and a half* knows something our ceiling is guessing at"; our own doubling stops at an hour.
- 2026-09-20 (TD-087): the usage reading moved to `usage.json`. It had lived in memory, so each promote forgot it and polled at once — eight times in one day. The first poll after a restart now waits until the held `fetched` plus the cadence.
- 2026-09-28 (TD-231 and TD-230, the designer; Paul: *our percentage used for the claude sub seems to be stale — our page reads 88%/95% but actual is 93% used*, *add how long ago the reading was made in the display*, *investigate the 429s*): usage became **reported first and asked for last**. Until then the one source was a poll of the tool's undocumented usage endpoint, every five minutes per account, and on 2026-09-28 it was refused for six hours: the held reading stood at 88% while the account was at 93%, the chip said *stale* and not how stale, and the gate, reading the same number against a line of 95%, could see no crossing. The anchor's research that day found no documented way to read a subscription's limits but the status line's `rate_limits`, and found the 429s widely reported with no usable `Retry-After`. So a session's status line reports what it is told, the endpoint is asked only for an account with no reading under fifteen minutes old and left alone an hour after a refusal, every reading carries its age, and the gate projects a reading older than `max_age` from the rate it last saw, pausing on the projection and resuming only on a reading. From the fact-check, which read the tool's documentation of the status line: a redraw repeats the last numbers, so reports are merged by what a window can do and a report's age moves only when the session has had a response; a pause on a projection must be able to end without a report, since paused sessions send none; `max_age` is a key of its own, `usage:`, because every key under `usage_gate` is a profile's name. Turned down: the rate-limit headers on model responses (undocumented), and asking the person each time a reading goes old (a night's question nobody is awake for). Build: TD-233.
- 2026-09-29 (TD-233 slice 3, grinder-ao-1): the usage endpoint became the fallback it was designed as. Until this date the host agent asked each account every five minutes and, after a 429, waited the endpoint's `Retry-After` floored at five minutes or doubled to an hour; on 2026-09-28 the endpoint refused for six hours with `Retry-After` 0 or none, so the doubling learnt nothing. Now an account is asked only when its reading is older than `USAGE_FRESH` (fifteen minutes) and at most once per `USAGE_FRESH`, and a 429 cools it off for `USAGE_COOL`, a fixed hour, a longer `Retry-After` kept; its end rides on the reading as `cool_until`, since the review found that a promote inside the hour would otherwise ask at once from the held reading's old `fetched`. `USAGE_EVERY` and `USAGE_BACKOFF_MAX` went. Until the report (slice 2) exists this is a fifteen-minute poll; the hourly ask for a window only the endpoint gives waits for the report, since until then every window comes from the same ask. Already true and not changed: each host asks for its own sessions' profiles, and `limited` skips a window past its reset.
- 2026-09-29 (TD-233 slice 2, the host agent's half, grinder-ao-1): the `usage_report` RPC, `sessionorc.usage` (the merge, the history, the hourly ask for a window only the endpoint gives) and each window's own `at`, `source` and `history` in `usage.json`. Two choices the design left open, written into §4.4 *The reading*: the endpoint's answer sets the windows it names outright, since it is the account's own number and a stale high report must not outlive it — the merge by the highest applies to reports; and two resets within five minutes are one window, since the status line's epoch seconds and the endpoint's instant never quite agree and a rolling window drifts. The caller of the RPC is the session the envelope names, so the identity check covers it as any other method. Not in this half: the status-line command and the adapter's `usage_report` (agentorc's), and a node's report to the home.
- 2026-09-29 (TD-233 slice 2, the adapter's half, grinder-ao-1): `agentorc-hook --statusline` and the launch layer's `statusLine`, with a refresh of sixty seconds. The field names were read from the installed client (2.1.285) rather than the documentation alone: `rate_limits.five_hour` and `.seven_day`, each `used_percentage` and `resets_at` in epoch seconds, and `cost.total_api_duration_ms`, the session's running total of API time, which is what the command reads for `fresh`; §4.3's `usage_report` is therefore a plain function returning that total and the tool's session id beside the windows, and the command, which holds the last-sent file, sets `fresh` from it — a new process under the same name counts from nothing, so a restart is fresh. The displaced line's `padding` has to be the layer's, since the tool draws with the layer's, so it is read at launch and the layer file gains a `+pad<n>` variant. A status line of ours named in a person's settings is passed over rather than chained, or the command would run itself. `limited` is read from the account's reading, so §4.4 *The poll, as built* now says *while nothing reports* of its fifteen minutes (the techlead's read of #770). Not built: a node's report to the home.
- 2026-09-30 (TD-233 slice 2, a node's report, grinder-ao-1): a node sends each report its sessions make on to the home as the link method `usage_report {id, account, windows, fresh}`, off the RPC's path and dropped with no link. The design left open whose account key the home uses; the node's, as `spend` already does, because the node holds the profile's credentials and a profile of one name may be another login at the home — keying it at the home would have let a laptop's `default` raise kmaster's account, and gains no protection, since the node names its own records' profiles anyway. So the home takes the key only in the record's adapter's namespace and for a record of that link's host, and a profile a home session runs under keeps the home's account, as a reading is per profile. The home shows the account while the node's session lives and never asks the endpoint for it. Not built: the home's send of the reading back to its nodes.
- 2026-09-29 (TD-233 slice 2, the home's send, grinder-ao-1): the home sends each account's reading back to the nodes that keyed a live session to it, as the link method `usage_reading {account, reading}`, on a change and once per new link. The design said only *as it sends the metered sums*; the sums travel as sums because a metered `pct` is the profile's, but a subscription reading is the account's, so the reading itself travels. How the node takes it was left open: not outright, since a report of its own may land between the home's merge and the send, and not as a report, since the home's reading carries the endpoint's answer, which may lower a number — so window by window, the newer confirmation or the later reset winning, with the node's own `reason` and cool-off kept because only the node asks for its account. Two gaps the techlead's read of #783 found were closed with it: a node's profile named metered at the home had its reports dropped, and after a home restart a node's account started clean, its history lost; the latter needed the passes before the node's first report to keep that profile's held reading, which they had dropped as no longer shown. A node's account the home does not show (its profile a home session's, or a second node's key) is kept while its session lives, since it is still sent back.
- 2026-09-17 (TD-066): one oversize `list` reply took every `ao` on the machine down at once — asyncio's 64 KiB default frame was smaller than a day's records, and the raise happened in the reader, which could say nothing about the cause. `FRAME_LIMIT` (8 MiB) on every stream, and the agent refuses to write a longer line, followed.
- 2026-09-17 (TD-062): version skew became a designed property. Until then the install was editable, so a merged RPC change was live at once (one broke `ao progress` for every worker for 31 minutes); once promoted, a merged change reaches every session's `ao` before the running host agent knows it. Drop-unset-parameters on the client and drop-unknown-parameters (`ignored: [...]`) on the agent closed the window for existing methods; new methods or changed meanings still need the promotion. The `ignored` line is accumulated across every call a command makes "since the call that skews is rarely the last one"; a caller bug against a same-age agent looks identical from the client, so the agent's log line (naming the method) tells the two apart.

The bound was applied one layer down from `_route_act`, where the reply is read; `AgentStuck` (a subclass) lets the one reconnecting caller distinguish a timeout (wedged agent, do not remake) from a drop (restart, remake).

## §4.4a (second half) — A container node; A node's records at the home; Acts across the link

- 2026-09-13 (§10): a devcontainer that runs an `agentorc-agent` beside a tmux server was ruled a host.
- 2026-09-17 (TD-057 step 3b): "A node's records at the home" designed and built — snapshot, then `report`/`gone`; `REPORT_EVERY` and `REPORT_WRITE` at 5 s; adoption of unseen records; `remote/<host>/`; the reachability overlay. The first thing the link carried.
- 2026-09-17 (TD-057 step 3c, after two Fable reviews and Paul's steer to the long-term shape): the container node designed — the home brings it up, installs the agent at its own version, keeps it running. The link socket, `ao host up`, the supervisor, occupancy and reach built the same day as 3c.1–3c.5.
- 2026-09-17: the reason the repo's `mounts` are dropped was contractmatch's own mount, which carries `.netrc`, a kubeconfig and a Modal token — the person's whole credential set. The tmpfs-at-same-target rule came from contractmatch's `postCreate.sh`, which creates a directory under such a mount under `set -e` and would have died on a missing path.
- 2026-09-17 (Paul): "the home installs the client, so it installs tmux" — hence the generated tmux layer rather than an edit to the project's Dockerfile.
- 2026-09-17: the tmux layer's first shape was a local devcontainer *feature* beside the generated file. Built, then refused by the devcontainer CLI: a local feature must sit under the workspace's `.devcontainer/`, which is the repo's, so it would have written into the person's checkout — the very thing the feature was to avoid. Replaced by two generated definitions (`base.json` tagged `agentorc-node-<name>-base`, then a one-stage Dockerfile `FROM` that base).
- 2026-09-17 (3c.4): cross-container occupancy built — `occupants()` at the home reads every container node's records over the directory while its link is up; a create routed with `--host` is checked at the home first, then at the node. `volatile: true` semantics for a person-stopped container (supervisor never starts the container, still starts the agent inside a running one) built as part of 3c.4.
- 2026-09-17 (3c.5): Reach built — `host_link.reach` from one look at docker, `docker exec … tmux attach` for the Focus terminal and `ao focus`, the `attached-container+` VS Code link.
- 2026-09-17 (TD-062): the promote gained one step, writing the wheel it installed to `~/.agentorc/wheels/`, from which a container node is provisioned. The image was required to supply Python 3.12+ because a feature cannot put an interpreter in every image the same way.
- 2026-09-17 (TD-057 step 4a): "Acts across the link" designed and built — the `act` link method, address rewriting in the reader's form, the gate reading one graph, home-owned edits applied only once the node has taken them in the same call, `create` with a `host`.
- 2026-09-18 (found live): a node provisioned before steps 4a, 5 and 4b stayed linked through five promotes, answering *unknown link method* to everything newer, because a promote changes no protocol number. Fix: a build is named by its wheel's content, said in `hello`, checked at `hello` and on every tick; a behind node is marked `stale` and re-provisioned and restarted by the supervisor, link up or not, after one grace (because a promote writes the wheel a second before it restarts the home, and a process about to be stopped must not start an install it cannot finish).
- Step 4 (org): `host:` on a team definition was a change to `org.yml`'s schema and `teams.plan`, so that `ao team start cm-grind` from kmaster lands the manager and the grinder in the container and the host limits the briefs encoded fell away.
- Step 4b.1: `ao tail` and `ao explain` on a remote record read its pane on its node via the `read` link method (`NODE_READS`); before this they were refused by name as not built.
- Step 4b.2: the general `intent` push (home → node) and `derived` reports (node → home) added. The per-call push in home-owned edits was kept beside it, because it is what makes an edit on an unreachable host a refusal rather than a divergence.
- 2026-09-19: `identity_ack` added to the `act` allowlist, its person-only check still running at the node (§4.8a).
- 2026-09-27 (TD-147, grinder-ao-1): *Settings, replicated* built — the `settings` link notification carries the home's `settings.yml` whole to every linked node after each `set_settings` write, and to a node once per dial; the node writes it as its own file (`_take_settings`). `set_settings` joined `modes.HOME_EDITS`, so a node forwards it while linked and refuses it offline in the home-owned edits' words. One choice the design left open: the dial's frame goes once the node's snapshot is taken, not inside the `hello` reply, since nothing is pushed to a link before its snapshot.
- 2026-10-04 (TD-316, grinder-ao-1): `ao host rebuild` and `ao host forget` refuse while the node holds a live record, naming them by team, with `--wind-down` and `--force` as the two ways on. Seen 2026-10-03 23:38 (TD-299): a rebuild of contractmatch ended grinder-cm-1 and manager-cm-1 mid-run with no wrap-up, their records gone `exited` as if the host had rebooted. The design said a rebuild is *on purpose* and what a gone container means, and not what a rebuild owes the sessions it ends.
- Not built (still, as of 2026-09-22): the terminal over the link for a machine node's session — *Later* in TD-057.
- Considered and rejected (undated, with the full reasoning): the UI host as a store-and-forward router was the least code but made the UI a second writer holding state and left unanswered which host gates a cross-host act; a mesh of host agents kept partial tallies and budgets that disagree after a partition, forced a sleeping laptop to accept inbound connections, and could not have a relay layered on it later; the relay as the bus now meant hosting the home elsewhere with a hosted service's login, tenancy and operations before there was a product. Prior art cited: Kubernetes control plane with node agents, NATS leaf nodes, IMAP over SMTP.

- 2026-09-29 (TD-221 slices 1–2, built by `grinder-ao-2`, *Boards are read against origin*): the board read passes the reader's `--fetch`, stopped at `BOARD_FETCH_TIMEOUT` (45 s) and followed at once by a plain read when stopped or failed, each board then carrying the reader's own *fetch skipped (<why>)*; each row keeps the reader's `source` and `fetch_note`. One fetching read runs at a time, in the background, and requests are answered from the last reading; the read after Snooze, Done, Reply or Put on the board is a plain read of that one board laid over it, and a fetch that began before the press keeps the pressed board's rows. The first read is plain and waited for — the design had not said, and a page that waits 45 s on a dead remote at start is the thing the bound is for. Built together, since slice 1 alone would have had every minute's request wait on the network.

## 4.5b Reachability: the person's own route, and the shape of a hosted service
- 2026-10-14 (ao-connect, with Paul): the guide gained the editor's step — the client on each computer the person codes from, and the ssh alias VS Code and `vscode_host` use pointed at the home's tailnet address. Found when Paul's VS Code on Windows still held kmaster's LAN address after the move to the tailnet; WSL's hosts script never reached it.
- 2026-10-14 (TD-648, grinder-ao-2): *The setting* built — `set_reach`, the one RPC that writes `reach:` (a person's own and the home's; the shape checked first: a known route, an `https` URL, a non-empty `allow`, `team` and `aud` for cloudflare; it answers what was there before), and `set_settings` refusing the key; an absent `notify.telegram.link` is `reach.url`, and the Settings page's link placeholder shows it, else `http://localhost:8765` (until this date `http://<host>:8765`, which a loopback plain port refuses). The phrases *until `ao connect` lands* and *not built* left this section.
- 2026-10-14 (TD-647 slice 2, grinder-ao-2): *An open websocket* built — the route listener's own task reads `reach:` every five seconds and judges each open route-port websocket again with the request it was let in with, closing it `1008` when the reading no longer lets it in (a removed `reach:`, a narrowed `allow`, a changed `url`); the layer closes it and hands the app its disconnect, so `/events` and `/term` end as on a closed tab. A broken `settings.yml` holds the last good reading for a minute, then refuses and closes until a read answers; a missing one is read as no route.
- 2026-10-14 (TD-647 slice 1, grinder-ao-2): *The route port* built — both listeners in one process (`shiftlead.ui.listener`: two `uvicorn.Server`s on one loop, one pair of signal handlers; the route port's socket bound by the layer and retried each minute), the Tailscale check, the plain port's proxy-header refusal, *Origin and Host* on both, `--route-port` and `--allow-host`, and `reach:`'s reader; the open websockets' following of the setting stays its second slice.
- 2026-10-13 (TD-646, ao-connect; Fable's review, adopted by Paul): Cloudflare moved from *offered second* to *designed, built when asked* (TD-656), and its token check is now to be decided together with the relay's passkey. A dated interim serve of the plain port was added, with its exposure stated. The Tailscale cell was *nobody in the middle who can read it*; it now also says Tailscale vouches for identity. Two paragraphs were added: cutting off a lost device, and why not a Unix socket. `listeners.json` was replaced by asking the port, and `--host` was renamed `--allow-host`, since *host* already means a machine here. The relay gained the passkey's hostname binding, its timing and volume view, and the person's own domain as its recommendation. Three Sonnet rounds followed, ending READY. They gave the interim a way off: the page names the manual steps until `ao connect` exists. They moved the `reach:` reader into TD-647's first slice. Fable's second round, adopted the same day, made these changes. The plain port's proxy-header refusal is now judged before `Host`; it was unordered. The route port reads `settings.yml` itself, and only on the home; it was through the host agent's `settings` RPC. `--allow-host` now applies on any bind; it applied only when `--bind` was not loopback. The Settings page's Telegram-link placeholder became `reach.url`. The interim's end may be an automatic promote. Every refusal is logged and counted on `X-Shiftlead-Refused`; only a bind failure was logged. Fable's third round (NOT READY) adopted three more. The tailnet access rule now grants 22 as well as 443, since the ssh that cures the interim needs it. A route-port refusal from a loopback `Host` is logged at `info`, uncounted, so the CLI's own probes do not count. The UI knows it is on the home by `hosts.is_node()`, since a node holds a replica of `settings.yml`. Fable's fourth round said READY.
- 2026-10-13 (TD-646, ao-connect, with Paul): rewritten around **the person's own route** — Tailscale offered first, Cloudflare Tunnel + Access second, `ssh -L` always — with shiftlead running nothing in the path, so each route works behind CGNAT. Added the UI's **route port** (8766), which requires the route's identity, and `ao connect`. Was (§4.5 *Security*, §10): a private network or an authenticated tunnel, either acceptable, with WireGuard on `vpnmaster` listed first; and (§4.5b) a `relay` that authenticated the person and proxied the UI, with a hosted UI as the *bring your own machine* product (§4.5c). Paul judged that a technical user would not route root-equivalent access through shiftlead's own servers, so a relay now forwards ciphertext only, and the home serves the UI and holds the login. Three Sonnet rounds followed: round 1 added the `Host` and `Origin` checks on both ports, against a hostile page riding the identity the proxy adds and against DNS rebinding. Round 2 had the plain port refuse proxy headers. Round 3 was READY once it was settled how the CLI learns the ports and how two listeners share a process.
- (undated, original draft): the section opened with "Why this is not 'install Tailscale'": for one person the private network is fine, but the deciding question is how someone who has never opened a port would use this.

- 2026-09-17 (§4.4a *A container node*): the container-on-the-home's-own-machine node was added to the `ssh` row (per-node link socket, directory bind-mounted in; home brings it up, installs its own version, supervises it).

## 4.5c Product direction
- 2026-09-06: written as "a paragraph, not a plan". At the time the claim that a hosted "run Claude Code for you" is what every model supplier already sells, and that neutrality is the moat, was a prediction.
- 2026-09-13 (amendment): the prediction came true — OpenAI's Agents API (public beta 2026-09-10), Anthropic's Managed Agents, AWS Bedrock AgentCore and Microsoft's Foundry Agent Service all sell a managed cloud agent runtime on token billing with no infrastructure fee. Conclusion recorded: the runtime is commodity; the relay sells the neutral view, not a runtime ([ADR](decisions/2026-09-13-openai-agents-api.md)). The spec now states this in the present tense.

## 4.8a Who is calling: identity on one host

- 2026-10-26 (TD-1064, the designer): *unknown* takes a peer in another pid namespace than the host agent's, so a container with `agent.sock` mounted into it is never the person; *A session never gains a person-only act by crossing a channel* says it host by host, and identity stays the channel's, never a credential the caller holds (TD-077's per-session secret, asked again; steered to Paul with that default). Built by TD-1093. §4.4a gains *A container that is no node has no `ao`*: such a container is made a node.
- 2026-10-26 (TD-1051, the designer; on contractmatch Paul's `! ao team stop` in a Claude Code pane was refused *needs the control grant*): *A tool's shell escape is the session's* — written down as what the ancestry rule already gives, with the refusal's cure for a person's session. TD-1080.
- 2026-10-16 (TD-801, the designer; Paul, 2026-10-16: *a shell should be considered my permissions*): *A process under the person's shell is the shell*: the wider right widens the same risk, left with the person. Built by TD-802.
- 2026-10-12 (TD-580, the designer): *A process under the person's shell is the shell* — an agent started by hand inside the pane inherits the person's acts, the person's own doing (Paul: out of scope); no narrowing to the pane's first process. Built by TD-596.

Under that unit the create path writes the pane's pid into `pane-<name>` in the server's cgroup (`identity.pane_cgroup`), and removes the empty `pane-*` directories the pane list no longer names. The `doctor` RPC's tmux reading gains `runs: system | user | none` (`identity.server_placement`).

Built by TD-495.

- 2026-09-17: the outage that motivates *observe before enforce* — one merged RPC change locked every worker out of `ao progress` for 31 minutes; a wrong ancestry rule would do the same with a worse cause, hence the `off | observe | enforce` modes and `observe` as the default for the release that introduced them.

Until this date every gate, §4.10's marks included, was what §4.8 says of the control gate — a guard, not a security boundary: a session could send as another session, and as the person, by changing or unsetting one variable (`AGENTORC_SESSION`), and the hook RPC trusted its `session` parameter the same way. Between hosts §4.4a's channel rule had always applied; this section brought it to one host.
- 2026-09-19: the host agent began reading `#{pane_tty}` beside `#{pane_pid}` in the tick's pane list (the third signal needs it).

A hook that still alarms now logs its peer, the record's listed pane and the gone one with its age, to tell a hook later than the grace from one that was never the session's.
- 2026-10-06 (TD-362, grinder-ao-1; filed from TD-360, its premise read on kmaster by the techlead): **a pane's own cgroup scope is the fourth signal**. tmux, built with systemd support, starts each pane in a `tmux-spawn-<uuid>.scope`, so no pane was in `agentorc-agent.service` and the detached check's *unknown* clause never fired. A session's process that shed ancestry, session id and terminal, such as a Claude Code background command orphaned by its setsid'd tool shell, read as *outside*: the person. It is now matched by its pane's scope, as a gone pane's hook is since TD-360. The *unknown* clause widens only to the scopes of our server's panes that no live record holds: a listed pane that is no record's, and a gone pane inside the grace. It was not widened to every `tmux-spawn-*` scope, since a person's own tmux server makes scopes of the same name (the techlead's narrowing of the grinder's steer). The sentence that `KillMode=process` keeps every pane inside the service was corrected.

Every ao-grind restart after TD-341 still alarmed *outside claimed <itself> on hook*. The peer's pid was below the new pane's, so it was the old run's `SessionEnd`, spawned as its pane was killed, not the new run's first hook. Claude Code starts a hook setsid'd with no terminal, so the orphan carried neither the gone pane's session id nor its terminal. On kmaster each pane runs in a `tmux-spawn-<uuid>.scope` of its own, which the orphan keeps. The grinder's default, refusing a hook that would be ignored with no alarm, was set aside: it classifies by the claim, and §4.8a never refuses silently.
- 2026-10-06 (TD-341, grinder-ao-1): **taking the name moves the old pane to the gone table at once**. Compared and not chosen: the reader handing the PR on to the next (a mover between stages, which a flow has none of, and a second way for mail to change hands beside `--pass-up`); the pass recorded as a PR comment in a fixed first line, as `cadence-review:` is (every session here is the person on GitHub, so the comment says nothing of who read — the mail thread does); a `pass` withdrawn by any later push to its paths (the home would have to read commits against comment times, and the last reader reads the whole diff anyway); per-role path sets (a path is held for what it is). The three choices a person might make otherwise — the author walks, the last reader merges, a pass stands — were steered to Paul. Not built.

- 2026-10-06 (TD-345): the words of Paul's that opened §4.9c until this day, verbatim: Paul (2026-10-04): *our current example is for a TD, which is something like [designer if needed] → [grinder + ui review if needed] → [techlead] → [escalate to me if needed], but I believe each repo is currently having to define this separately. It seems prudent to have the flow defined once then reused, and to give the ability to create more flows*; *flows would be per team*. On the first draft: *"read" comes across too passive, the techlead is doing real work*; *is the escalation to me (when needed) inferred?*; *it seems odd to say a team is going to use a flow but then does not staff the right roles — have an alert that the flow cannot be followed and change it or choose a different flow*. On the second: *my concern is that we do all of this work to define flows and then we have to hand-jam any changes anyway. Would it make more sense to keep a set of briefs with each flow so that a team could switch flows on the fly? It makes sense that a flow would have to be well-defined before being usable.* And on the third: *the high level goal is to be able to define roles, and use those roles in flows. We will likely end up with a small list of roles and flows, and flows will naturally need certain types of roles, but outside of that the two should be essentially orthogonal. Eventually we will let people create additional roles/flows through the UI but that does not have to happen yet. We just want the design to be able to handle it.*

- 2026-10-09 (TD-459, the designer): **a lapsed cache is started again, not rung** — a member the doorbell has decided to ring, idle past `CACHE_LIFETIME` (1 h) with a context over `CACHE_FLOOR` (100k), is restarted on its brief by rule 7's tick restart under its precondition, `why: cache`; the restart is the wake; seats, nodes and a person's session left out; `read_when`'s idle sentence says which. ADR 2026-10-08 option 3, Paul's decision. Built by TD-467.
- 2026-10-06 (TD-347 slice 2, grinder-ao-1): **the bell** built — `doorbell_held`, `mail.DOORBELL_HELD`, the ring judged at its turn's `Stop`, a read or a person's act lifting it, and *doorbell held · n unread rings* on `ao status -v`'s mail line. Decided in the build: a ring's count is remembered before the line is typed, because the tool's `UserPromptSubmit` for the ring landed before the submit confirmation returned and the ring's turn went uncounted (found by the build's own test, intermittently); a ring is judged only once its prompt has been seen, so a stray `idle` between the ring and its turn counts nothing; and the run lives in the host agent, so its restart starts the count again rather than holding a bell on a run it did not see.

- 2026-09-13 (§10): manager-to-manager messaging was closed "by accident rather than by decision" — the `control` grant (named `orchestrate` until TD-055 step 3) plus `controllers` was the only gate, and keystrokes (`ao send`) the only delivery, so messaging had been folded into control. That accident was the tell that led to the split: of the four kinds of traffic only manager-to-worker worked; a worker reached upward through `progress`/`findings` (declarations, not a channel); two managers were peers and TD-036's gate refused them each other; two workers coordinated by side effects (a ledger row, a branch name, a PR claiming the reference). Diagnosis: "a conflation, not four missing features."
- 2026-09-14: section written. First draft said a message never starts a turn (an idle session stayed idle with mail waiting; a sender needing work to begin used `send`). Paul called it too blunt — it left mail useful only to a session already blocked in `ao wait`, i.e. managers, and two workers could message each other into inboxes neither would read — so a message may wake, metered by a budget.
- 2026-09-14 (Paul): "Where the line actually is, since it is thinner than 'mailbox versus pane'" — naming the delivery mechanism made the distinction look like an implementation detail; mediation and attribution are the two properties actually claimed.
- 2026-09-14 (Paul): "Portability: the mailbox is core, surfacing it is the adapter's job" — mail joins the adapter contract rather than assuming one tool's shape.
- 2026-09-14 draft: the first draft said the wake budget was restored by a controller's send and by any turn mail did not start; review found the loop that permits (worker mails manager, manager's `ao wait` returns, manager `send`s, the worker's `send`-started turn "resets" it, worker mails again, every turn counting as work) and cut both.
- 2026-09-14 draft: let a worker message "a person" and amended invariant 5 to allow it, but gave no edge that reached one. Fable review 2026-09-16 replaced it with the per-org person inbox rather than inventing a *creator* edge.
- 2026-09-16 (Fable review, round one): the wake budget defined as mail-caused wakes in a rolling window; a `wait` returning because of mail counts, so managers are not the unmetered half of every loop. Round one charged `ao wait`'s mail returns, but `ao wait` ran wholly in the CLI, watched only the caller's members and never its own inbox, and the host agent never learned why it returned — a manager out of budget would have been woken by every message.
- 2026-09-16 (second review): the host agent decides each wake at the reachable moment; `ao wait` becomes the host-agent RPC `wait`. Second review also removed `out_of_work` from the "pending stop beats mail" list — the first 2026-09-16 text listed it there and contradicted §4.9a.
- 2026-09-16 (rounds two and three): a `send` made inside a mail-caused turn was charged to the controller's budget and refused when spent, with the wrap-up prompt exempt.
- 2026-09-16 (fourth review, reversing the second): a controller's `send` is never charged. The rule only doubled the price of a cycle already bounded by the manager's wake charge, added a refusal mode (a manager mid-turn could not instruct its own worker), an exemption, a definition of where a manager's turn ends, and a hole — `ao wait --timeout 0` put a manager outside a mail-caused turn and let it `send` for free.
- 2026-09-16 (fourth review): "a decision not to wake advances nothing" — the `mail_decided` mark stays put when the budget is spent, otherwise a refilled budget would never ring for mail that landed while spent. Also: a refusal at the person inbox names `user_attention.md` with a `Due:` date, so it is a redirect, not a dead end.
- 2026-09-16 (Paul): "Other tools' own messaging is left alone" — Claude Code's cross-session `SendMessage` is not switched off; people already use it (ADR decisions/2026-09-16-agent-messaging-prior-art.md).
- 2026-09-16 (Paul): the doorbell — a fixed line the host agent rings, never the sender's words — was added because the rules said a message *may wake* but named no way to do it for the one adapter that exists.
- 2026-09-16 draft: had the `Stop` hook *block* the stop while mail was unread. Fable's review cut it: it saved one paste and a few seconds, and cost a synchronous round trip to the host agent on every `Stop` of every session (`Stop` is fire-and-forget with a 3 s timeout, `hook.py`) plus `stop_hook_active` handling and stop-beats-mail checks in a second place — "the one change that could slow every session, for the smallest gain."
- 2026-09-16: Paul asked for a reminder when a session keeps reporting with mail unread; review reshaped it from a count of reports (which misses a worker that reports only at claim and at done) to a line on every `ao` command's output.
- 2026-09-16 (TD-052 step 2): a session's `reply` to a person's message, naming no addressee, lands in the person inbox.
- 2026-09-16 (TD-052 step 3, as built): mail's half of the wait cursor is the `mail_decided` watermark; a wait returns mail as headers only; a person's session in `wait` is never returned by mail; the `wakes` list `{at, cause, charged, covered}` on the record.
- 2026-09-19: an `ask` to the person stopped expiring — until then it expired read or not, like any other kind.
- 2026-09-20 (TD-052 step 7, as built): doorbell on every tick as its own task; `wrapup_at` stamped by a `send` marked `wrapup` (Wrap up on the card and Focus, `ao team stop`) and cleared by the next plain send; `_decide_wake` recorded `via: doorbell`; one ring per idle stretch; the retry into an empty composer only; `doorbell_failed` (`{at, error}`) in `ao status -v`; the line is `sessionorc.mail.unread_line`.

Until this date one set — every entry unread or an open question — was held to 200 in all and 100 from one sender, and a person's read set no `read_at`, so a note counted until it was dismissed: on 2026-10-04 techlead-ao-1's verdict on held PR #1040 was refused with 100 slots held by its own notes, and the anchor dismissed them by hand. The poll that found nothing is now one that also leaves nothing unread: the end-the-turn line needs the reply's unread count at 0 as well.

The build reads it as ten minutes after the *and more* line, when everything sent before it has left the window, and §4.10 says so.
- 2026-10-05 (TD-319 slice 1, grinder-ao-1): **the send built, and a backlog is never told.** The design said when a row is told but not what becomes of one already standing when the switch is turned on, or that stood through a home that was down: told at once, six at a time behind the burst's *and more*, would be a message about something the person could already see. The build tells a row only while its hold ended within `NOTIFY_LATE` (5 min), which covers a restart and leaves out a backlog, and §4.10 says so.

What the design added to the entry's rule (*only what Needs you counts, on a transition into it, never twice, not while the page is focused*): the home is the sender, since the Inbox's sections are composed in the UI, which runs wherever it is installed (§10) and so may run more than once; told is narrower than counted — what stops a session or a team, not a promote row that would ring at every merge; a minute's hold; a message carries no text a session wrote; and the token never enters the host agent's environment — a child under `doppler run` holds it for one request. - 2026-10-15 (TD-685 slice 2, grinder-ao-1): *Sync*'s pass built as `agent_sync`, on the promote's full readings, with steps 3 to 5 in `sessionorc.sync` (`candidates`, `decline`, `judge`, `mark`). The `held:` globs it checks are the repo's `.shiftlead.yml` `held:` (§4.9c), and a file that cannot be read is no reading. The pass runs as its own task. An unread `gh` login judges nothing that pass, and a green PR with no verdict is held back from the order only while a pass covered its repo inside `SYNC_COVER` (three readings). A merge refused under a moved head writes nothing. A switch turned off writes *off* at each unjudged head, and *off* is no verdict, so turning it on again judges the PR. A merge `gh` refuses, or a head unread before the merge, is no reading and counts a try. TD-684's order reads the outcome through `sync.mark`: `sync_home` (merged, or green and unjudged while the switch is on) is no order, and `sync_why` is the order's reason. `repos.<repo>.sync.auto` is settable. A `held:` written as named sets is their union (the techlead's read), and an *off* PR's order says *sync is off*.
- 2026-10-14 (TD-685 slice 1, grinder-ao-1): *Sync*'s check built as `sessionorc.sync.check(root, number, head, branch, clones=, held=)`, steps 1 and 2 as §6 words them, off the loop and reading git alone: the lock's source against the base's, its clone among the registry's checkouts, `files_commit` on that clone's default, each lock-listed path the PR changes against its line and each changed line against dev-cadence's `files/` at `files_commit`; then the replay in `~/.shiftlead/sync/<repo>/tree` at the merge base, `post_sync` from the base's `docs/cadence.toml` under `SYNC_BOUND` with `PATH`, `HOME` and `LANG` alone, the lock's membership (what `post_sync` wrote excepted) before the comparison with the head, then the held globs. It answers *mechanical*, *refused* with the first reason, *error* (the home's own failure, no reading) or *moved* (origin's head is not the one asked about, so nothing was checked). A lock line the head drops must name no file at `files/<path>` at `files_commit`, else *lock not dev-cadence's: <path>*, so a PR cannot drop a guard script's line and delete it; whatever `post_sync` leaves running is killed with its group on every road (the review of slice 1).

- 2026-10-14 (TD-681, the designer): §6 *Sync* — the home merges a mechanical sync PR, one it has checked:
  - it is not forked, its author is the home's own login, and its repo has a gate (a PR failing any of these is *refused* at once, with nothing posted);
  - every lock line that differs from the base lock's is checked against dev-cadence's `files/` at `files_commit`, and each changed file's bytes against its line;
  - it deletes no path the base lock never listed;
  - the replay at the merge base runs the repo's `post_sync` with a scrubbed environment, and the tree equals the head;
  - it touches no held path.

  The home then posts a `cadence-review: SHIP · sync-check` comment, runs the gate in the registry checkout, and squash-merges pinned to the head after re-reading the head and the holders. Only a gate fail (exit 1, or a `gate:` non-zero) posts BLOCK and hands the PR to the team; a check with no reading is tried `SYNC_TRIES` times. - 2026-09-22 (TD-103; Paul chose option 1 of the design review): the four mechanical rules of the manager's brief — crash restart under the 3-in-2-hours ceiling, the wanted restart, seat fills, the idle nudge — become host-agent policies keyed on `unattended` and a new `supervised` field, under *a restart is not a start*; the restart ceiling and the fill ceiling become constants; `supervised`, `seat`, `seat_due`, `restarts`, `restart_ceiling`, `restart_blocked` and `nudged_at` join the home-owned fields; a launch record (`launch/<id>.json`) is written at every supervised create. Sonnet round 1 (READY WITH CHANGES, six findings, all adopted): rules 2 and 3 gained *not gated*; the manager is supervised too, and its `ao close` at wind-down is not a crash; an idle seat with `seat_due` is nudged; `restart_blocked` clears itself when the work is pushed while `restart_ceiling` waits for a person; a failed replay counts toward the ceiling with `why: failed`; `supervised` survives Resume and is cleared only by Forget. Round 2 (READY WITH CHANGES, five findings, all adopted): a failed replay keeps its `why` and adds `error`; `restart_blocked_sent_at` is home-owned; the fill ceiling's mark lands on the seat that tripped it; the mode toggle's row names the supervision rules; the stop-time policy's per-record isolation is a target, not a fact. Round 3 (READY WITH CHANGES, two findings, adopted): rule 1 excludes seats (a seat's natural exit is not a crash; rule 3 alone fills one); invariant 14 carries the caveat §4.9a had. Round 4 (READY WITH CHANGES, three findings, adopted): invariant 9 names `supervised`; rule 3 carries *not suspended*; a person's Resume clears `restarts` with the mark. Round 5 (READY WITH CHANGES, one finding, adopted): §4.8 says a director's managers are supervised and the tick, not the director, restarts one. Round 6 (READY WITH CHANGES, one finding, adopted): the launch record is written at every create whose record carries `supervised`, attended or not, so Hand back after a Resume with changes replays the latest choices. Round 7 (READY WITH CHANGES, one finding, adopted): rule 2 restarts only an idle member or a natural exit, never a kill, a Close or a session past its stop time. Round 8 (READY WITH CHANGES, one finding, adopted): §4.9a's controller rule drops `closed` to match. **Closed by Fable after round 8**: eight rounds, and from round 3 on each round's one finding was a consistency follow-on of the previous adoption rather than a new hole; the anchor judged the text implementable and recorded the override here rather than run a ninth round. Until then: §4.9a said *the host agent starts nothing by itself* and the manager's brief carried the rules.
- 2026-09-22 (TD-103 slice 1, grinder-ao-1): `supervised` and the launch record built — the field on the record (home-owned), `ao team start` setting it on every session it creates, `ao new --supervised`, `launch/<id>.json` (owner-only) written at every supervised create — at the home for a node's session, under its address — and removed on Forget. A resume keeps `supervised` from the record of its name or of its conversation, in the host agent, so no client has to carry it; a fresh, unsupervised create that takes a supervised record's id removes the stale launch record.

- 2026-09-22 (TD-103 slice 3, PR #459, grinder-ao-1): rule 3, the seats, built on the home's tick — `seat_due` from `seat`, the fill with `keep_mail` replaying the launch record (`why: fill`), `FILL_CEILING` (6 an hour over seats sharing a controller) and the idle seat's close; TD-104 folded in. Three points the design had left open were settled in the build and written into rule 3 (a steer to the techlead, default taken): `by` names what met the trigger; the count before it is met is a new home-owned `seat_count`, since `seat_due` exists only once met; the home reads `gh` in the seat's checkout at the same absolute path, and a path it cannot see gives no reading. The two-minute `SEAT_IDLE_GRACE` was added so a fill is not closed before its prompt lands. The same PR made rule 1's *not gated* read the profile's usage, since the gate clears `gated` on an exited record and the check had been true for every crash. The parked `td104-seat-due` build (PR #444) gave the outage-is-not-zero rule and the card's count.

Rule 4 types the fixed nudge once per idle stretch, recorded on `sends` as `system`, and the card reads *idle · open work* twenty minutes after that.
